findings.title: KeyError when the existing Integration has no `sender` metadata
findings.body: `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every pre-existing Integration carries webhook-provided `sender` metadata. `build_integration` only sets `sender` from `state.get("sender")`, and nothing in this pipeline ever binds that key. The updated `test_basic_flow` also shows an Integration created through the pipeline with no `sender` in its metadata. If such an Integration remains without an OrganizationIntegration, for example after one org is uninstalled, a legacy record, or an install created through the pipeline, this lookup raises `KeyError`. The user gets a 500 instead of the friendly error page, and the install is blocked. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and treat a missing sender as a controlled failure, or define explicit behaviour for it.

findings.title: Authenticated-user check is skipped whenever the Integration row doesn't exist yet
findings.body: The new `github_authenticated_user` vs `sender.login` comparison only runs when an Integration with that `external_id` already exists. It is created by the `installation` webhook. When `Integration.DoesNotExist` is raised, the code calls `pipeline.next_step()` without checking that the OAuth-authenticated user is the one who installed the app. Anyone who learns an installation_id can therefore finish the pipeline before the webhook has been processed, or if it was delayed or lost, and bind someone else's installation to their org. The check depends on a webhook race. A robust fix would verify against GitHub directly, for example by confirming the installation appears in `GET /user/installations` for the user token. The OAuth user token is already available at that point but is discarded after reading `login`.

findings.title: OAuth `state` is a static, guessable value, so it gives no CSRF protection
findings.body: `state` is `pipeline.signature`, which the tests pin to the constant `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3`. That is a deterministic hash of the pipeline view classes, not a per-flow random nonce. Every user and session therefore gets the same value, and an attacker can craft `/extensions/github/setup/?code=...&state=<known>` links that pass the check. An OAuth `state` must be unpredictable and tied to the user's session. Also, `!=` is a non-constant-time comparison; use `constant_time_compare`. As written, the PR's claim that a mismatching `state` is rejected adds little real protection.

findings.title: Network and HTTP errors in the token exchange and user lookup are not handled
findings.body: Only `safe_urlread` and decoding are inside the `try`. `safe_urlopen(...)` on line 423 can raise connection, timeout or SSL errors, and `get_user_info(...)` on line 434 calls `raise_for_status()`, so an invalid or expired token raises `HTTPError`. Either failure surfaces as an unhandled 500 in the middle of the install dialog, not the 'Invalid installation request' page the PR describes for these cases. The existing `OAuth2CallbackView.exchange_token`, which this code is modelled on, wraps the whole exchange in exception handling. The failure paths also log nothing, so a failed exchange gives support and debugging no signal.

findings.title: `test_installation_not_found` no longer exercises the installation-not-found path
findings.body: The test now sends `state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05`, which differs from the pipeline signature `9cae5e...`. The request is therefore rejected by the `state` mismatch check in `OAuthLoginView` before the 404 from `/app/installations/...` is ever reached. It asserts the generic 'Invalid installation request.' text. So it now covers state mismatch under a misleading name, and the `The GitHub installation could not be found.` branch in `build_integration` has lost its coverage. Use the valid state for this test, and add a separate test for state mismatch.

findings.title: New failure and success paths of the validation are untested
findings.body: Only the user-mismatch case is covered, and only incidentally the state mismatch. There are no tests for: a failed token exchange (no `access_token` in the response); a `/user` response without `login`; or the positive case where an Integration with webhook-provided `sender` already exists, has no OrganizationIntegration, and the authenticated user matches. That last case is the main new success path of `GitHubInstallation`. There is also no test for an existing Integration lacking `sender` metadata, which would currently raise `KeyError`. `assert_setup_flow` additionally hard-codes `responses.calls[2]`, which silently breaks whenever the number of HTTP calls in the flow changes.
